newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's new anti-Islamist government faces future.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's new anti-Islamist government faces future.

text.p: Turkey's new ruling secularist politicians turn their attention on Sunday to the challenge of reuniting a country torn by religious and political divisions after winning a confidence vote.
The new anti-Islamist government sealed its grip on power after Saturday's rowdy vote that had mirrored rifts in the country.

Parliament voted 281 to 256 to approve a coalition under Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz that is designed to keep the big Islam-based Welfare Party at bay and end months of social and political tensions over the role of religion in public life.
Turkey, a Western ally, has exposed some of its raw nerves in a year-long search for identity under an Islamist-led government that collapsed last month.

The conservative Yilmaz has vowed to guide the country back to the uphill road to integration with Europe. He has also promised to restrict Islamic education -- one of the most sensitive issues in the battle for the country's hearts and minds.
Yilmaz was conciliatory after the vote.
"We know Turkey has very serious problems but there is no issue our country cannot solve with tolerance, compromise and the power you have given us," he told parliament.
"The first step we will take is to return everything to normality. Our nation is sick of disputes," said Yilmaz, 50.
The last months of predecessor Necmettin Erbakan's tenure were marred by fierce public debate over Islam, democracy and the right of the influential army to play politics.
Erbakan resigned last month amid fierce military criticism of his attempts at mild Islamist reforms and his closeness to Moslem Iran and Libya.
Analysts say Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party, the biggest single party in the fractious parliament, will be a tough opposition for Yilmaz, who has been prime minister briefly twice before.
"Turkey is facing the danger of moving step by step towards chaos and confusion," Erbakan told a news conference on Saturday.
He predicted a key left-wing party would withdraw its support from Yilmaz's minority coalition once the government began tp backtrack on a promise to hold early elections in 1998.
"This government does not have the staying power, so it is obviously not going to get anywhere," he said. "Let's see how many days it will last. You'll notice I am talking about days."
Most commentators say the Islamists would do well at early elections and want to go to the polls as early as possible.
The party is facing closure by the constitutional court for allegedly threatening Turkey's secularist system in a case expected to last another four months.

Despite winning the confidence vote, Yilmaz's hold of power does not extend to control of some key parliamentary committees where the Islamists and their conservative allies could still frustrate his secularist agenda.
